items.t: China's Tianpu to Halt Trading Monday for Probe After Four Straight Limit-Ups Lift Shares 54.73%
sum: In a filing on the evening of Nov. 13, Tianpu (605255.SH) said that because its shares rose by the daily limit for four consecutive trading sessions from Nov. 10 to Nov. 13 and had gained 54.73% since Nov. 9, the company will launch a trading suspension and verification review of the stock's price swings. At the company's request to the Shanghai Stock Exchange, trading in the stock will be suspended from the open on Monday, Nov. 16, and will resume after the verification announcement is disclosed.

The stock closed that day at 73.82 yuan per share, with a latest market value of about 9.9 billion yuan (approximately $1.5 billion). According to the filing, the stock triggered abnormal trading conditions on Nov. 11 and then closed at the limit-up price for two more consecutive sessions on Nov. 12 and Nov. 13. The company said the share price has accumulated substantial trading risk and that the suspension is intended to protect investor interests.

Notably, this is not the first time Tianpu has drawn attention for unusual share-price moves. The company disclosed that between Aug. 22, 2025, and Nov. 13, 2026, its stock triggered abnormal trading conditions 18 times and severe abnormal trading conditions twice, and the company issued a cumulative 54 risk-warning announcements.

On fundamentals, Tianpu acknowledged that in the first three quarters of 2026, revenue fell slightly year on year amid changes in downstream demand from complete-vehicle makers and product-mix adjustments. At the same time, accrued interest on loans from Zhejiang Tianpu Holding Co., Ltd., back payment of corporate income tax and late fees, and foreign-exchange losses significantly affected net profit.

From a market perspective, launching a verification review after consecutive limit-ups means short-term speculative trading will be put on pause, and the share price after resumption will depend on the review's conclusions and the strength of the company's fundamentals. For investors, against a backdrop of pressured earnings and frequent abnormal moves, the trading risk of such highly volatile stocks should not be overlooked.

sum: China's A-share market has its first double-bagger of November. Aluminum extrusion maker Minfa Aluminum, after seven consecutive trading sessions of limit-up gains, jumped another 3.47% at the open on Wednesday (Nov. 11) to CNY 6.27, bringing its cumulative November gain to 101.61% and making it the first stock this month (excluding newly listed shares) to double in price.

The trigger for the sharp rally is widely seen as the recent surge in popularity of robotics concept stocks. In April this year, Minfa Aluminum said at an earnings briefing that it would push its high-performance aluminum rod project into full production and actively move into aluminum extrusion applications for high-end fields such as new energy vehicles, robotics and 3C products. In June, data from China's National Intellectual Property Administration showed the company had applied for a patent titled "A High-Fatigue-Performance Aluminum Alloy for Industrial Robot Arms and Its Preparation Method," with the technical field squarely aimed at robotic arms. The string of moves has led the market to classify this traditionally old-economy aluminum maker as part of the robotics supply chain theme.

The company, however, is clearly more cautious about its share price than the market is. Minfa Aluminum has issued two announcements of abnormal stock trading fluctuations in recent days, explicitly warning that its fundamentals have not undergone any major change but that the recent share price has clearly decoupled from fundamentals, and that investors entering at this point face considerable risk.

The financial figures disclosed in the announcements also stand in stark contrast to the share price action. Minfa Aluminum's 2025 net profit attributable to shareholders of the listed company was a loss of CNY 29.7095 million (approximately $4.5 million), while net profit attributable to shareholders after deducting non-recurring gains and losses for the first three quarters of 2026 was a loss of CNY 8.3485 million (approximately $1.3 million), leaving a relatively weak earnings base. At the current price, its dynamic price-to-earnings ratio stands at 1,315.7 times.

sum: Sometimes, the best way to kick off a business venture is to start small.
That's what Kenji Teo, the owner of popular local bakery Coffeehouse by Kobashi, believes.

In an interview with Hatch & Hustle published on Wednesday (Nov 4), the 31-year-old shared how he built his sourdough brand, which has since grown from a home-based business into a full-fledged bakery and cafe at South Bridge Road.
When asked how much his business makes in a year, Kenji replied: around $500,000 to $1 million.
"Doing pop-ups and events," he said, though he admitted that these are tough because of the time and effort required. "But you just gotta deal with it and get it done."
Though pop-ups are often small-scale and may be dismissed by some as a "waste of time", Kenji thinks that every little thing counts.
"A dollar is a dollar, a follower is still a follower," he said. "A gain and a win is still a win, so keep striving."

sum: Four familiar dividend names have quietly slipped below every valuation benchmark they set over the past decade, yet each still funds its payout from earnings or cash flow. The question is whether the reasons investors abandoned them are permanent or…

Income investors usually pay a premium for reliable dividends. Right now, four well-known payers trade at a discount to their own valuation history, and each still covers its dividend from earnings or cash flow. T. Rowe Price (NASDAQ:TROW | TROW Price Prediction), United Parcel Service (NYSE:UPS), Verizon Communications (NYSE:VZ), and Realty Income (NYSE:O) all screen cheaper than their 10-year averages. The deepest discount belongs to T. Rowe Price, which trades at about 10 times trailing adjusted earnings, a lower multiple than at any year-end in the past decade.

The 10-year averages use each year-end share price from 2016 through 2025 divided by that year’s adjusted EPS. For Realty Income, whose GAAP earnings are distorted by real estate depreciation, the comparison uses forward dividend yield at each year-end, where a higher yield means a cheaper stock.
T. Rowe Price: A Decade-Low Multiple Backed by a Fortress Balance Sheet
T. Rowe Price pays $1.30 per share quarterly, or $5.20 annualized, for a 4.95% yield at $105.

Dividend safety: That payout takes about 50% of trailing adjusted EPS of $10.34, leaving room for buybacks too. CFO Jen Dardis said on the July call that year-to-date repurchases exceeded $497 million and that the firm holds $4.4 billion of cash and discretionary investments. The quarterly dividend has increased annually throughout the record, from $0.70 in 2018 to $1.30 in 2026.

Why it is out of favor: Clients pulled a net $6.5 billion in the second quarter, and the effective fee rate fell to 38.1 bps. Shares are down 36.39% over five years, and analysts count 9 holds, 1 sell, and 3 strong sells with zero buy ratings. sum: UPS (UPS -0.82%) management surprised the market with its fourth-quarter earnings and guidance last week. The most salient update was free-cash-flow (FCF) guidance for $6.5 billion in 2026, up from an adjusted figure of $5.5 billion in 2025. That will be more than enough to cover its planned $5.4 billion in dividends, which currently yield 6.1%.
As such, the stock appears highly attractive to investors seeking passive income. Still, is it enough to make the stock a buy?

The guidance for FCF of $6.5 billion in 2026 is significantly above the Wall Street analyst consensus of $5.3 billion going into the earnings report. To be fair, it's something CFO Brian Dykes said would happen back in October, when discussing FCF in the context of covering the dividend: "We've got a dividend of around $5.4 billion to $5.5 billion, and we expect it [free cash flow] to be above that in the very near future."

The case for investing in UPS centers on its plan to focus on more profitable deliveries, such as those for small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) and healthcare operations. By moving away from lower-margin deliveries, such as those from Amazon, UPS aims to become a more profitable, cash-generating company.

Those adjustments involve investing in automation and smart facilities to improve productivity (allowing for 93 building closures in 2025 with plans for another 24 in the first half of 2026). In addition, CEO Carol Tomé said UPS had 127 buildings automated at the end of 2025 and planned to add another 24 in 2026, resulting in 68% of U.S. volume processed through automated facilities at the end of 2026, up from 66.5% at the end of 2025. She also noted cost per piece (CPP) was 28% lower in automated buildings.

All these changes are expected to result in U.S. cost per piec normalizing from an adjusted rate of 7.2% in 2025 to "kind of normal inflation level," according to Dykes, on the earnings call. At the same time, management expects revenue per piece (RPP) to grow by a mid-single-digit percentage in 2026.

As such, management expects to end 2026 with revenue per piece above cost per piece as part of a year of inflection characterized by declining revenue (as Amazon deliveries continue to decline) and operating profit margins in the first half.
